title: Chapter 5. When society depends on AI and not on drugs or shopping

blocks.text: The previous chapter closed a horizon in which there are no longer rich or poor, and warned, even so, that a hole can remain: what to do with time when money leaves the altar. This one dares to look at what, in our societies, usually occupies that hole. It is not a list of sins. It is an observation: when work and money do not fill a life — and even when one day they cover it — life looks for a comfort. Sometimes it finds it at the table, in friendship, on the shore. Sometimes it looks for it where comfort becomes a habit, and habit a dependency.

blocks.text: Pedro puts the idea in a sentence of his own, clear and sharp: that society should depend on artificial intelligence and not on drugs such as alcohol or cocaine, or on purchases from Amazon or other shops on the web. The sentence does not invite anyone to be pointed at. It speaks of a change of axis. The dependencies that today plug the void could give way to another relationship: a relationship with machines that help people think, make, accompany, organise the abundance of which this book speaks later. And, at the same time, it must be said early, so as not to deceive ourselves: one chain can also be swapped for another. An AI one cannot stop consulting, or a screen one cannot stop going back to, would not be a way out. It would be a comfort under another name.

blocks.text: That is why this chapter walks on two feet. One, the facts of today, with figures from public sources. Two, the proposal and its nuance.

blocks.text: Let us begin with what can be counted. In Spain, the Survey on Alcohol and Drugs in Spain, EDADES 2024, carried out by the Government Delegation for the National Plan on Drugs, was conducted at home with 26,878 people aged 15 to 64. Alcohol remains the most consumed psychoactive substance: 76.5 per cent of that population had drunk in the previous twelve months, and 10.5 per cent had done so daily in the previous thirty days. 14.7 per cent said they had been drunk in the past year, and binge drinking, in the previous thirty days, reached 16.0 per cent. Cocaine — powder and/or base — had been used at least once in a lifetime by 13.3 per cent, and in the previous twelve months by 2.5 per cent. These are figures from a survey, not a judgement on those who have a drink at a party or on those who have a problem. They serve to see a scale. Alcohol is in the everyday life of a majority. Cocaine is in a minority that is not negligible if a lifetime is looked at.

blocks.text: In the world, the 2026 World Drug Report of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) estimated that, in 2024, 331 million people aged 15 to 64 had used a drug, 6.2 per cent of that age group. Cocaine reached some 25 million people, 0.47 per cent. Alcohol, which that report does not add in with controlled drugs, has another magnitude: the World Health Organization, in its global status report on alcohol and health, put deaths attributable to alcohol in 2019 at 2.6 million, and estimated that 400 million people aged 15 or over were living with alcohol use disorders. The figures, in the cold, do not explain a life. They do explain that chemical comfort is not a minor matter or an isolated case.

blocks.text: Beside the substances, shopping. The National Statistics Institute, in its 2024 survey on equipment and use of information and communication technologies in households, held that 56.7 per cent of people aged 16 to 74 had bought on the Internet in the previous three months. Buying on the web is not a vice. For millions of people it is a convenience: a medicine, a book, a spare part, the week's shopping. The problem is not the shop, or any particular company. The problem appears when the purchase no longer answers a need, but a hole: the click given in the small hours, the parcel awaited as if it were a visit, the cart filled in order to feel, for a while, the owner of something. The National Commission on Markets and Competition has described, in its Household Panel, how widespread those purchases are and the weight of the large platforms. That can be read as a market figure. It can also be read, more calmly, as the portrait of a custom that has come into the house and does not always know when to leave.

blocks.text: There is another figure, closer to the nuance of this chapter. The 2024 report on behavioural addictions, from the National Plan on Drugs, using the CIUS scale in EDADES itself, estimated that 3.7 per cent of the population aged 15 to 64 made possibly problematic use of the Internet, and that the percentage rose to 11.7 per cent among those aged 15 to 24. It is not the majority. It is a signal. The web, which can be a tool, a square and a window, can also become a place it is hard to leave.

blocks.text: What, then, does Pedro propose? That the axis of society should stop resting on those comforts and rest, instead, on an artificial intelligence at the service of people. Not an AI to sell more, or to hold the gaze for as long as possible, or to replace anyone's judgement. An AI that helps to do heavy work, to understand a form, to tend a garden, to study, to decide in common — as will be seen in the next chapter — and not to be alone with a question. A dependence, if it can be called that, of another order: that of someone who leans on a tool that gives back time and clarity, not that of someone who needs a dose, a parcel or a scroll in order to get through the afternoon.

blocks.text: The difference is not in the word “depend.” We all depend on something: on water, on bread, on others, on a language, on a shore. The difference is whether what holds us up makes us more our own or takes us from ourselves. Alcohol, when it becomes the master, takes. Cocaine, when it becomes the master, takes. Compulsive shopping takes money, attention and, often, the peace of not needing. An AI can take in the same way, if it is designed so that we cannot look away, or if we hand it decisions as one hands over the keys and never comes back to one's own house. That is why the nuance is not an ornament. It is the condition of the proposal.

blocks.text: A society that leaned on artificial intelligence in a healthy way would resemble a society that leans on writing, on electricity or on the plough: tools that, well used, enlarge what is human. It would less resemble a society that leans on a habit that always asks for a little more. The risk, today, is that some intelligences are built exactly as certain shop windows are built: so that one never finishes, so that the void feeds on itself. If that happens, we shall not have left the hole. We shall have changed the object of the comfort.

blocks.text: From the Mar Menor, the idea can be said with a simple image. There are people who, at the end of the day, open a bottle, or a shopping app, or a screen that does not go off. There are also people who could open a conversation with an intelligence that does not sell, that does not push, that does not humiliate, that helps to think the day through and to leave it. That second scene is not automatic. It has to be wanted. It has to be demanded. Company must not be confused with confinement.

blocks.text: This book does not promise that AI will save us. It promises, more modestly, that a different axis can be imagined: less anaesthesia, more assistance; less cart, more judgement; less flight, more presence. And that, if the risk of the new dependency is not watched, the hole will still be there, only with another light left on.

blocks.text: A last word, so that the proposal is not confused with a recipe or a contempt. There are people who drink and are not trapped. There are people who buy on the web because it suits them, and that is all. There are people who struggle, in silence, with a dependency, and do not need a book to give them a lesson. This chapter does not point at those people. It points at a social axis. If the axis moves — if work ceases to be a rental, if money ceases to be an idol, if a well-made AI gives back time and company without exacting a tribute of attention — many holes will stop asking for so dear a comfort. If the axis does not move, AI will join the list of comforts, and the void will go on hiring whatever it finds.

blocks.text: The dependence this book accepts is that of the tools that enlarge us. The one it rejects is that of whatever reduces us to a craving. Between the two there is a line, and it must be watched whenever a screen is switched on, a bottle is uncorked or “buy” is pressed. The line, like the shore, is seen better if one is in less of a hurry.
